newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD attacks Waigel's budget plans.
newsitem.headline: German SPD attacks Waigel's budget plans.

text.p: A key opposition Social Democrat (SPD) on Thursday attacked the government's budget plans, saying Bonn had abandoned its goals of fighting joblessness and pushed higher debt burdens on to future generations.

SPD budget spokesman Karl Diller told journalists that Finance Minister Theo Waigel exceeded constitutional limits with the higher deficit contained in his supplementary budget for 1997, details of which became known earlier on Thursday.
It and the 1998 budget, both of which Waigel is to present to the cabinet on Friday, rely too heavily on privatisations to meet revenue goals, Diller said.

"The principle of a sustainable security in state finances has been thrown overboard, and burdens have just been postponed for the future," Diller said. "Waigel's bridge to 1999 does not rest on a secure bank, it hovers above the abyss."

The 1997 supplementary budget foresees a deficit of 71.2 billion marks, up from 53.3 billion marks in the original plan. In 1998, the deficit is seen falling back to 57.8 billion marks. Privatisation revenues in 1998 are seen rising to 19.7 billion marks from 12.7 billion marks this year.
Waigel said last week that Germany was still in line to meet the fiscal goals for European monetary union despite the higher 1997 deficit.
While the SPD had demanded since February that Waigel present a supplementary budget, Diller said the plan Waigel has come up with did too little to create jobs.
It also forces Waigel to declare that the government has lost its grip on the economic balance, as the constitution requires if the deficit exceeds government investment, he said.
"There are no conceptual grounds (for such a declaration) in this supplementary budget," Diller said.
The SPD will oppose the government's plans to cut the solidarity tax, since they would force states to give up 3.5 billion marks in revenue.
The coalition's tax reform plans, now being debated in parliament' mediation committee, would cut revenued by about 20 billion marks a year, placing additional pressures on the deficit, Diller said.
Its pension reform plans would cost another 15 billion marks a year.
